newsitem.title: GERMANY: CDU says Germans must be better informed on euro.
newsitem.headline: CDU says Germans must be better informed on euro.

text.p: A leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said on Tuesday the German public need to be better informed about Europe's planned single currency, the euro, due to be launched in 1999.

The remarks coincided with the publication of a poll showing that most Germans were afraid that the introduction of Europe's single currency will lead to higher inflation and reduce the value of their savings.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze hailed an agreement reached on Monday at a European Union summit in Amsterdam to support a so-called stability pact, to enforce fiscal discipline among countries that join the launch of the euro.
The pact was originally proposed by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to dispel fears among the German public they might be swapping their mark for a potentially softer currency.
"With the stability pact it is an unshakeable fact that the euro will be as a hard a currency as the mark," Hintze said.
"(But) I am aware that much more must be done to inform the German population. The CDU will intensify its publicity work about the euro in a summer information campaign about Europe.
"I am sure the euro will soon draw the same emotional power as the D-mark. The euro will be both a reliable currency and a symbol of close cooperation in Europe," Hintze said in a statement.

The survey of some 1,500 Germans carried out by the EMNID institute for Frankfurt-based investment broker DAVG found that 64.4 percent of respondants believed the euro would hurt their savings. Nearly 62 percent thought Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) would lead to higher inflation.

Bonn has already launched an information campaign including a tent currently touring Germany where the public can ask staff questions and receive leaflets about EMU. Bonn has opened telephone hotlines for public inquiries.
The European Commission has sent a boat up the Rhine river with a floating exhibition to sell Germany's mainly sceptical public on the advantages of the euro.

The exhibition, which set sail from Rotterdam on June 2 and will end its tour in Strasbourg in mid-July, argues that the history of money in Europe has been a process of simplifying multiple currencies to culminate in the euro.
